context_before.text: In considering a family of HEAs that are of relatively similar composition, but which present a significant difference in electrochemical performance (especially in terms of passivation), the polarisation response of such a selection of alloys is shown in Fig. 4. The alloys presented (Fig. 4) are CoCrFeNiAl, CoCrFeNi (SPS^) and $\mathrm { T i } _ { 0 \cdot 3 } (\mathrm { C o C r F e N i }) _ { 0 \cdot 7 }$ in 0?6 M NaCl. As with all the HEAs surveyed, the alloys shown in Fig. 4 are ‘spontaneously passive’ in 0?6 M NaCl. In addition, these alloys all have very similar cathodic reaction kinetics. The cathodic kinetics are more rapid than those of $(\mathrm { T i A l }) _ { 0 \cdot 7 } \mathrm { V } _ { 0 \cdot 1 5 } \mathrm { F e } _ { 0 \cdot 1 } \mathrm { N i } _ { 0 \cdot 0 5 }$ and AlTiVCrSi (Fig. 2), and hence, it is posited that the presence of Co enhances the cathodic kinetics and concomitantly raises the $E _ { \mathrm { c o r r } }.$

The microstructures of $\mathrm { C o C r F e N i A l _ { 0 }. _ { 9 }, }$ CoCrFeNi (SPS^) and $\mathrm { T i } _ { 0 \cdot 3 } (\mathrm { C o C r F e N i }) _ { 0 \cdot 7 }$ are also provided in Fig. 4, while the associated electrochemical parameters are presented in Table 3. The difference in the electrochemical properties of the alloys is that the passive window $(E _ { \mathrm { p i t } } - E _ { \mathrm { c o r r } })$ size scales according to $\mathrm { T i } _ { 0 \cdot 3 } (\mathrm { C o C r F e N i }) _ { 0 \cdot 7 }$ $\mathrm { > ^ { \bullet } C o C r F e N i A l _ { 0 \cdot 9 } ~ > C o C r F e N i ~ (S P S ^ { \wedge }) }$. This result is interesting on the basis of the conventional wisdom that relates to corrosion and merits comment. The largest window of passivity correlates to the alloy variant that contains Ti, which is conventional in its own right. However, it is unique when considered with the microstructure. The very large passive window of $\mathrm { \cdot T i _ { 0 \cdot 3 } (C o C r F e N i) _ { 0 \cdot 7 } }$ persists in spite of a very heterogeneous microstructure (at least three unique phases) and significant segregation. The phase denoted as ‘A’ in the BSE image of $\mathrm { T i _ { 0 \cdot 3 } (\hat { C } o C r F e N i) _ { 0 \cdot 7 } \quad (F i g. } \quad 4 g)$ is enriched in Ti $(\sim 6 2 { \cdot } 8 \mathrm { a t } \mathrm { - } \%)$ with the associated energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) point analysis shown in Table 4. In the case of CoCrFeNi (SPS^), the microstructure is also multiphase, with the fine black dots in Fig. 4e that are actually synonymous with very fine pores. As noted, CoCrFeNi (SPS^) exhibits a significantly lower $E _ { \mathrm { p i t } }$ compared to CoCrFeNi (AM). In addition, the i ofCoCrFeNi(SPS^) $(0 { \cdot } 6 1 0 \mu \mathrm { A } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 })$ is significantly larger than that of CoCrFeNi (AM) (0?108 mA cm<sup>22</sup>). CoCrFeNi (AM) is a single fcc solid solution, as indicated by the XRD spectrum in Fig. 5a. On the other hand, CoCrFeNi (SPS^) exhibits a multiple phase microstructure with the corresponding XRD spectrum, as shown in Fig. 5b, indicating that it consists of an fcc and sigma type phase (s). Praveen et ${ \cdot } a l. ^ { 4 3 }$ reported that CoCrFeNi sintered at 1000uC using SPS consisted of a major fcc phase and a minor Cr rich sigma phase. This sigma phase could be a CrFe/CrCo/CrFeCo intermetallic compound.<sup>43</sup> EDS mapping results for CoCrFeNi (SPS^) are provided in Fig. 6, confirming that the sigma phase is rich in Cr, while the fcc matrix is Cr depleted. In austenitic stainless steel, the s phase is an intermetallic compound with a complex tetragonal structure. The s phase is rich in Cr, with a typical normalised composition of the s phase being Fe $(\sim 5 9 \mathrm { \ w t - \% }),$ Cr (*38 wt-%) and Ni $\left(\sim 3 \: \mathrm { w t - \% } \right). ^ { 4 4 }$ In stainless steel, Cr rich sigma phase has a detrimental effect on the corrosion resistance including pitting resistance.<sup>24</sup> Similar to the effect of Cr rich sigma phase in stainless steel, the evolution of a Cr rich s phase in CoCrFeNi (SPS^) is also detrimental. The Cr rich s phase is nobler than the adjacent Cr depleted fcc matrix, therefore rendering the Cr depleted matrix susceptible to corrosion.

context_after.text: In the case of CoCrFeNiAl <sub>?</sub>, this alloy exhibits a fine interconnected microstructure, which is unique on the basis of the connectivity of microstructural features. $\mathrm { C o C r F e N i A l _ { 0 \cdot 9 } }$ is comparatively very noble in 0?6 M NaCl and also exhibits a low corrosion current density compared to the other HEAs listed in Tables 1 and 3. In contrast to the posit that the presence of Co enhances cathodic kinetics and concomitantly raises the $E _ { \mathrm { c o r r } },$ a simpler microstructure is also associated with a high $E _ { \mathrm { c o r r } },$ albeit on the basis of reduced anodic kinetics. The instance of reduced anodic kinetics correlates with a low corrosion current density, as depicted by $\mathrm { C o C r F e N i A l _ { 0 \cdot 9 }. }$ The XRD spectrum for as cast $\mathrm { C o C r F e N i A l _ { 0 }. _ { 9 } }$ is shown in Fig. 7a. The as cast $\mathrm { C o C r F e N i A l _ { 0 \cdot 9 } }$ consists of a combination of fcc and bcc phase, not excluding that the latter may be in the form of the B2 phase (which is an ordered bcc phase). The bright field (BF) image of $\mathrm { C o C r F e N i A l _ { 0 }. _ { 9 } }$ is provided in Fig. 7b, and the select area diffraction pattern (SADP) of the dark contrast phase along the [011] zone axis is provided in Fig. 7c and is consistent with a B2 phase with a lattice parameter of 0?3001 nm. The SADP of the light contrast phase along the [011] zone axis in Fig. 7d is consistent with an fcc phase with a lattice parameter of 0?3704 nm. $\mathrm { C o C r F e N i A l _ { 0 \cdot 9 } }$ exhibits a simple microstructure (fcc B2), and there is no segregation of elements, like Cu in Cu containing HEAs or Cr in CoCrFeNi (SPS^), that could deteriorate the corrosion performance of the HEA. The simple microstructure and no elemental segregation could be associated with the relatively high corrosion potential and small corrosion current density of $\mathrm { C o C r F e N i A l _ { 0 }.. }$.

context_after.text: Future avenues of work in order to provide a more comprehensive determination of the corrosion of HEAs should pay particular attention to the following aspects.

The microstructures of HEAs present features that span the atomic scale to the tens of micrometre scale (*6 orders of magnitude). The area where the least characterisation exists to date is in the nanoscale, and therefore, HEAs should be examined by high resolution techniques such as atom probe tomography and high resolution TEM. Of the works to date that have studied nanostructure, useful insights have emerged, as one study<sup>45</sup> employs three-dimensional atom probe (3DAP), revealing the presence of fine Cu rich precipitates, Al–Ni rich plates and Cr–Fe rich features in cast AlCoCrCuFeNi HEA.
